title: Business case: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge whether a project is developing, checking, maintaining and confirming its business case properly, and pick the reason that fits the scenario.
question: Tarnside College's deputy principal for finance says the grant award proves the Engineering Skills Centre is worthwhile, so no business case is needed. Is this appropriate, and why?

teach.h: Is the justification still sound, and is anyone checking?
teach.body: Formally, the business case practice establishes mechanisms to judge whether the project is, and remains, desirable, viable and achievable, to support decisions on continued investment. In plain English: someone must keep asking 'is this still worth it?' at the right moments, using the latest numbers. A BL4 question describes how a project handles its business case and asks whether that is effective. The answer turns on the develop, check, maintain and confirm technique and on who acts when.

steps.label: Develop
steps.sub: Outline in SU, full in IP

teach.body: The project mandate triggers the outline business case in starting up; it is refined into the full business case in initiation and approved by the board when it authorizes the project. Options analysis always starts with 'do nothing differently', the baseline for quantifying 'do the minimum' and 'do more than the minimum'. The difference between them is the benefit the investment buys. Even compulsory or externally funded projects must justify the option chosen.

teach.h: Who checks the business case, and when
head: Who
When they check it
rows: End of IP: authorize the project
Each stage end; any exception plan
At the end of the project
teach.caption: Checking asks whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable as costs, timescales, products and risks become clearer.

teach.body: Maintain: at the end of each stage the project manager updates the business case with progress (products delivered, costs, benefits realized) and the latest forecasts, so the board can check it before authorizing the next stage. Confirm: assessing whether the intended benefits have been, or will be, realized. Most confirmation happens after closure, through post-project benefits reviews run by the business; the project only plans them. Some benefits may be realized earlier when products are released in increments.

Benefits reviews planned for the business

rows.label: Check
values: Once at the start, then filed

teach.text: Two classic traps. First, a benefit only counts if it flows from outcomes enabled by THIS project's outputs; savings from a separate scheme do not belong in this business case. Second, the project does not run post-project benefits reviews: it plans them in the benefits management approach, and the business carries them out after closure.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Tarnside College's skills centre
teach.body: Leah Whitfield, the project manager, is in delivery stage 3. The vice principal asks for 30 welding bays instead of 24. Before anyone decides, Leah assesses the effect on the business case: extra cost against a 3% overspend limit, extra apprentice places, and the risk to the fixed September opening. At the end of the stage she updates the business case with actual spend and new forecasts so the board can check it before authorizing stage 4. Both are sound business case practice.

items: Name the step being applied: develop, check, maintain or confirm.
Check the timing: is it at the right process, stage boundary or trigger?
Check the role: board checks at decision points; PM prepares, maintains and checks impacts.
Decide the verdict from the scenario facts, then pick the reason that actually explains it.
Reject reasons that are true in the manual but do not explain this situation.
All projects need a business justification, usually a business case; funding or compulsion is not a substitute (5.1, 2.1).
Options are quantified against 'do nothing differently' (5.3.1.1).
The board checks at each decision point; the PM checks when assessing risks, issues and changed objectives (5.3.1).
The PM maintains the business case at every stage end (5.3.1).
Benefits are confirmed mostly after closure, by the business, using reviews the project planned.

summary: You can now judge whether a project is developing, checking, maintaining and confirming its business case effectively. You can pick the reason that explains the verdict rather than a true but irrelevant statement.

A.q: Tarnside College is starting up its Engineering Skills Centre project. Project manager Leah Whitfield compares three options: leave the warehouse empty and keep sending apprentices to other providers, a basic refit with 24 welding bays, and a full refit with 30 bays. She measures the costs and benefits of the two refit options against the first. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because there are three basic options to consider for any investment
Yes, because doing nothing differently is the baseline for the other options
No, because a grant-funded project does not need to analyse its options
No, because options are compared after the full business case is approved
A.why: 'Do nothing differently' comes first and is the basis for quantifying the other options; the difference between them is the benefit the investment buys (5.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: It is true that there are three basic options, but that does not explain why the refits are measured against leaving things as they are.
whyNot.2: Every project must justify its chosen option, including grant-funded and compulsory ones (2.1).
whyNot.3: Options analysis is part of developing the outline business case in starting up, before the full business case.

A.q: Tarnside College's skills centre is in delivery stage 3. The vice principal for curriculum asks for 30 welding bays instead of the planned 24, which would add cost against the governors' 3% overspend limit. What should project manager Leah Whitfield do first about the business case?
options: Assess the effect of the request on the business case justification
Update the expected benefits to show the extra apprentice places
Ask the contractor to price the six extra bays and start on them
Send an exception report to the board about the possible overspend
A.why: The project manager checks the business case when assessing issues and risks, weighing extra benefit against extra cost and risk before the change is decided (5.3.1, 2.1).

whyNot.1: The business case should not be changed to assume a benefit from a change that has not been assessed or approved.
whyNot.2: Starting work on an unapproved change bypasses issue control and any check of the justification.
whyNot.3: An exception report is needed when stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded; the effect has not yet been assessed.

A.q: At the end of stage 3 of Tarnside College's skills centre, Leah Whitfield revises the business case with the actual spend to date, the latest cost forecast for fit-out and the confirmed apprentice pledges, ready for the board. Which step of the business case technique is she applying?
options: Check
Develop
Confirm
Maintain
A.why: Maintain: at the end of each stage the project manager updates the business case with progress data and the latest forecasts (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: Checking is the assessment of whether the project is still desirable, viable and achievable, which the board does with the updated case.
whyNot.1: Developing produces the outline and full business case in starting up and initiation.
whyNot.2: Confirming assesses whether benefits have been, or will be, realized, mostly after closure.

B.q: Tarnside College's skills centre is in its final stage. A governor asks that the project stays open for a year after opening so that project manager Leah Whitfield can measure apprentice numbers and report whether the benefits were realized. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Plan the reviews in the benefits approach for the college to run after closure
Extend the final stage by twelve months so the project can measure the benefits
Record the twelve-month review as a quality activity in the quality register
Add the apprentice review as a product in the plan for the final stage
B.why: Running post-project benefits reviews is not a project activity; the project plans them by updating the benefits management approach, and the business carries them out (5.3.1, 19.2).

whyNot.1: A project should close cleanly; benefits confirmation continues outside the project lifecycle.
whyNot.2: The quality register records quality activities on products, not benefits reviews.
whyNot.3: Benefits reviews happen after closure, so they are not products of the final stage.

B.q: During stage 4 of Tarnside College's skills centre, heat pump prices rise and the forecast cost now exceeds the stage tolerance. The board asks Leah Whitfield for an exception plan, which includes an updated business case. Should the board check the business case when it reviews the exception plan, and why?
options: Yes, because the executive is responsible for securing the project's funding
Yes, because assessing an exception plan is one of the board's checkpoints
No, because the board already checked the business case at the end of stage 3
No, because the project manager checks the business case when assessing issues
B.why: The board checks the business case at the end of starting up, at the end of initiation, at each stage end and when assessing an exception plan (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: It is true that the executive secures funding, but that does not explain why the board checks the business case at this point.
whyNot.2: A stage-end check does not cover the new forecast; the exception plan is a separate point at which the board checks.
whyNot.3: It is true that the PM checks when assessing issues, but that does not remove the board's check of the exception plan.

B.q: Tarnside College's sustainability manager proposes adding to the skills centre business case an expected benefit of a 20% carbon cut across the whole campus, most of which will come from a separate boiler replacement scheme next year. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the business case should reflect the college's ESG goals
Yes, because expected benefits must be measured against today's position
No, because the benefit would not result from this project's outputs
No, because carbon targets belong in the sustainability approach instead
B.why: Projects deliver outputs that enable outcomes that realize benefits. A cut that comes mostly from a separate scheme is not a benefit of this project (5.1).

whyNot.0: Alignment with ESG goals matters, but it does not make another scheme's carbon savings a benefit of this project.
whyNot.1: Benefits are measured against today, but that does not explain whether this benefit belongs to this project.
whyNot.3: A measurable carbon cut caused by this project could be an expected benefit, so the location is not the problem; the real problem is that this cut would come from another scheme.

C.q: Tarnside College is starting up its skills centre project. The deputy principal for finance says that because the combined authority has already awarded a £4.2 million grant, the college does not need a business case: the grant agreement proves the project is worthwhile. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because external funding confirms the project is desirable
Yes, because the grant agreement already states the expected outcomes
No, because the grant can be clawed back if apprenticeships start late
No, because every project needs a business justification it can check
C.why: All projects must have a business justification, usually documented in a business case, developed in starting up and refined in initiation, so it can be checked throughout (5.1, 5.3.1.1).

whyNot.0: Funding does not show the project is viable and achievable, nor that the chosen option offers best value.
whyNot.1: A grant agreement is not a substitute for the project's own justification that the board checks at each decision point.
whyNot.2: The clawback risk is a scenario fact, but it does not explain why a business case is needed.

C.q: Tarnside College's skills centre has five stages. To save the board's time, Leah Whitfield proposes updating the business case only when the project is authorized and again at closure, not at the end of each delivery stage. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because manage by exception reduces the time the board must spend
Yes, because the full business case is baselined in the PID at authorization
No, because the board must check an updated business case at each stage end
No, because benefits are confirmed by the business after the project closes
C.why: The PM maintains the business case at the end of each stage so that decisions at stage boundaries are checked for continued business justification (5.3.1, tab 5.2).

whyNot.0: Manage by exception saves board time through tolerances, not by skipping the stage-end check of justification.
whyNot.1: The business case is baselined, but it must still be maintained and checked at each stage boundary.
whyNot.3: It is true that benefits are confirmed after closure, but that does not explain why the stage-end updates are needed.

C.q: During stage 2 of Tarnside College's skills centre, an offshore wind operator cuts its pledge from 40 apprentice places a year to 20. Leah Whitfield notes this in the daily log and plans to look at the business case at the end of the stage, four months away. Is this an appropriate application of the 'business case' practice, and why?
options: Yes, because the business case is updated at the end of each stage anyway
Yes, because benefits are confirmed mainly after the project has closed
No, because the PM should check justification when stakeholders' aims change
No, because the board must approve a new business case before work continues
C.why: The project manager checks the business case when assessing risks and issues and when stakeholders' objectives change, so the effect on justification is known early (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: It is true that the case is updated at stage ends, but that does not justify waiting four months to assess a change that affects benefits.
whyNot.1: It is true that most confirmation is after closure, but that does not explain delaying the assessment of a change now.
whyNot.3: The board decides at stage boundaries or on exception; the PM's first step is to assess the impact.

reteach.title: Think of the business case as a living argument
reteach.question: If the business case were a court argument, when would it be written, re-tested and finally proved?

blocks.body: The case is written in outline before initiation and in full during initiation (develop). It is re-tested whenever a decision is due or the facts change (check), after the PM has brought the evidence up to date at each stage end (maintain). It is finally proved when the benefits arrive, mostly after closure, through reviews the business runs (confirm).

explain.body: The outline business case is developed in starting up from the mandate and refined into the full business case in initiation; the board approves it when authorizing the project. Options are quantified against 'do nothing differently'.

test.q: Tarnside College's outline business case for the skills centre compares a 24-bay and a 30-bay refit with each other, but never with continuing to send apprentices elsewhere. What is the main weakness?
options: No baseline to quantify the benefit of investing
The full business case has not yet been approved
The senior user has not specified the benefits
The sustainability targets are not yet costed
test.why: 'Do nothing differently' is the basis for quantifying the other options; without it the benefit the investment buys cannot be measured (5.3.1.1).

whyNot.1: The full business case comes later, in initiation; that is not the weakness here.
whyNot.2: Benefits specification matters, but the stem describes missing options analysis.
whyNot.3: Costing sustainability is not the issue described.

explain.body: The board checks at the end of starting up, end of initiation, each stage end and when assessing an exception plan. The PM checks when assessing risks and issues, at project end and when stakeholders' objectives change.

test.q: Tarnside College's skills centre has just finished initiation. Which check of the business case should happen now?
options: The PM checks it when assessing the risk register
The board checks it to authorize the project
The business checks it in a benefits review
The senior user checks it to authorize stage 2
test.why: At the end of initiation the board checks the full business case when deciding whether to authorize the project (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: The PM checks when assessing risks and issues, but the end-of-initiation check is the board's.
whyNot.2: Benefits reviews confirm benefits, mostly after closure.
whyNot.3: Authorization is a board decision, not the senior user's alone.

explain.body: At the end of each stage, in managing a stage boundary, the PM updates the business case with products delivered, costs, benefits realized and current forecasts, and assesses aggregated risk.

test.q: Tarnside College's stage 4 is ending. Who should update the business case with actual costs and new forecasts before the board considers stage 5?
options: The executive
Project assurance
The project manager
The senior user
test.why: Maintaining the business case at stage ends is the project manager's job, on the executive's behalf (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: The executive owns the business case but does not maintain it.
whyNot.1: Project assurance may review it, not update it.
whyNot.3: The senior user specifies benefits but does not maintain the business case.

explain.body: Confirming assesses whether intended benefits have been, or will be, realized. It mostly happens after closure through benefits reviews run by the business, planned in the benefits management approach.

test.q: Tarnside College's skills centre has closed. Who carries out the reviews of whether 300 apprentices a year are being trained?
options: The project board
The project manager
The project team
The business
test.why: Post-project benefits reviews are carried out by the business after closure; the project only plans them (5.3.1).

whyNot.0: The project board exists only for the life of the project.
whyNot.1: The PM's role ends at closure.
whyNot.2: The project team has been disbanded at closure.
